newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Congress posts worst environmetal vote record.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Congress posts worst environmetal vote record.

text.p: The 104th Congress' environmental voting record improved in its second year, but the Republican-led Congress still was the most anti-green ever, the League of Conservation Voters (LCV) said Tuesday.
In its legislative "scorecard," the league said 44 lawmakers finished with zero ratings because they were on the wrong side of all the major contested environmental votes.
At the end of 1995, 135 members had zeros out of the total of 535 members in the House and the Senate.

"It's worth noting that some of the Republican freshmen who scored very low in 1995 did begin voting for the environment to boost their re-election chances with angry constituents," said Deb Callahan, president of the league, which acts as a political arm of environmentalists.

But at a news conference she said, "This scorecard confirms that the 104th Congress was simply atrocious on the environment -- the most extreme Congress on this issue we've seen since we started the scorecard 26 years ago."
Callahan said 137 lawmakers scored in single digits in this Congress, up 243 percent from the 56 low-scoring lawmakers in the 103rd Congress.
The Senate averaged 46 percent pro-green votes, with Democrats averaging 84 percent and Republicans averaging 13 percent, the scorecard said.
The House averaged 46 percent, with Democrats averaging 74 percent and Republicans averaging 20 percent, it said.
One of the low-scoring House Republicans, Richard Pombo of California, issued a news release calling the league "an arm of the Democrat Party, plain and simple."

"LCV has spent 96 percent of its funds in this election cycle in support of its fellow Democrats. Ninety-four percent of their endorsements have gone to their liberal Democrat cronies. To call this a bipartisan organisation is a joke," Pombo said.
Republican presidential candidate Bob Dole, in his last two years as a Kansas senator, scored a 4, the league said.
But Callahan stressed that the league saw "champions in both parties" who fought efforts to roll back environmental laws, and killed many of the anti-green bills.

The 104th Congress ended up passing several major environmental measures including safe drinking water protections, pesticide law reforms, and measures to halt over-fishing and restore the nation's fisheries, but those were not recorded in lawmakers' scorecards.
Callahan said they were not contested bills by the time they reached the House and Senate floors, and votes in their favour did not signify environmental support.
"That's saying you're going to go along with the crowd. This scorecard is about making tough choices," she said.
